Every partner is an agent of the firm for the purpose of its business.
Subject to any agreement, a partnership is dissolved by the death of a partner.
bank.question: Under the Partnership Act 1890, which THREE of the following are true of a general partnership?
bank.explanation: Partners in a general partnership have unlimited liability and are agents of the firm; the partnership usually dissolves on the death or bankruptcy of a partner unless agreed otherwise.
Adverse possession requires factual possession (exclusive physical control) and the intention to possess the land to the exclusion of others, including the paper owner.
options: The squatter must have the permission of the legal owner.
The squatter must have factual possession of the land.
The squatter must demonstrate an intention to possess the land.
The squatter must have paid the council tax on the property for at least 5 years.
The land must be registered at the Land Registry already.
bank.question: To claim title to land via adverse possession, which TWO of the following elements must the claimant prove?

bank.explanation: Homicide requires the person to be 'in being' (born alive); an unborn foetus or a person legally brain dead are not generally subjects of homicide.
bank.question: In the law of murder, who is considered a 'person in being' for the purpose of the actus reus? Select TWO.
options: A human being who has been born alive.
A human being who is not yet 'brain dead' under medical legal standards.
A foetus in utero.
A person who has already been declared legally dead by a doctor.

bank.explanation: Under s.2(1) of the Act, a person is not guilty of theft if they believe they have a legal right, the owner's consent, or the owner cannot be located by taking reasonable steps.
bank.question: Under the Theft Act 1968, which THREE of the following scenarios describe a person who is NOT to be regarded as dishonest?
options: The defendant believes they can make better use of the property.
The defendant believes they have in law the right to deprive the other of it.
The defendant believes they would have the other's consent if they knew of the circumstances.
The defendant believes the person to whom the property belongs cannot be discovered by taking reasonable steps.

bank.explanation: Under the PACE Codes, an intimate search may only be authorised if there are reasonable grounds for believing the person has concealed a Class A drug or a weapon.
options: A Class A drug which they intended to supply.
An article that could be used to cause physical injury.
Items of clothing that may serve as forensic evidence.
Stolen high-value jewellery.
bank.question: According to PACE Code C, an intimate search of a suspect in custody may only be authorised by an inspector if there are reasonable grounds for believing the person has concealed which TWO of the following?
Under the SRA Code of Conduct, a solicitor may only act for two or more clients where there is a conflict of interest (or a significant risk of one) if which TWO of the following conditions apply?
options: The clients are long-standing family friends of the solicitor.
The solicitor is able to act in the best interests of each client.
The clients have a 'substantially common interest' in relation to the matter.
The clients are 'competing for the same objective'.
bank.explanation: Solicitors must not represent two or more clients where there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, unless the limited exceptions (substantially common interest or competing for the same objective) apply.

options: The relief of poverty.
The funding of high-quality art for a private collector's home.
The advancement of education.
The advancement of religion.
bank.question: To be legally classified as a charitable trust, the purpose must fall under a recognised head of charity. Which THREE of the following are recognised heads of charity?
bank.explanation: The trust must be for the relief of poverty, the advancement of education, or the advancement of religion (among other defined heads) to be charitable. High-quality art for a private collector is not a public benefit.

Private medical records and communications with a religious advisor are generally considered 'excluded material' under PACE and require a specific warrant from a judge, not just a standard search warrant.
bank.question: Under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE), which TWO of the following are classified as 'excluded material' and require a special procedure for access?
options: Personal records which a person has acquired or created in the course of any trade or profession which they hold in confidence.
Stolen laptops and electronic equipment.
Journalistic material which a person holds in confidence.
Items used in the commission of a burglary.

bank.explanation: To file for a summary judgment, the applicant must show the other party has no real prospect of succeeding and there is no other compelling reason for a trial.
options: The claim has a 50% chance of success at trial.
The claimant or defendant has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim or issue.
There is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at a trial.
New evidence has come to light since the disclosure stage.
bank.question: Under the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR), a court may give summary judgment against a claimant or defendant if which TWO of the following conditions are met?
According to the Law of Property Act 1925, which TWO of the following are the only legal estates in land?
options: An estate in fee simple absolute in possession.
A term of years absolute.
An easement for a period equivalent to a life interest.
A restrictive covenant.
bank.explanation: Under the Law of Property Act 1925, legal estates are limited to the fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold).

options: Maximize the profit of the law firm in every transaction.
Follow all instructions from the client even if they are illegal.
Act with integrity.
Act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the solicitors' profession.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following are mandatory SRA Principles that apply to all solicitors?
bank.explanation: The SRA principles require solicitors to act with integrity and in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the solicitors' profession.

bank.question: When a court determines any question with respect to the upbringing of a child under the Children Act 1989, which TWO of the following principles apply?
options: The child's welfare is the court's paramount consideration.
The parent's financial status is the primary factor.
The court shall not make an order unless it considers that doing so would be better for the child than making no order at all.
The court must always award joint custody to both parents.
bank.explanation: Under the Children Act 1989, the child's welfare is the paramount consideration, and the court will also consider the 'no order' principle (making an order only if it is better for the child than not making one).

bank.question: In a standard criminal trial, who bears the legal burden of proof and what is the standard of proof required for a conviction? Select TWO.
options: The prosecution.
The defendant.
On a balance of probabilities.
Beyond reasonable doubt (so that the jury/magistrates are sure).
bank.explanation: In a criminal trial, the prosecution bears the legal burden of proving the defendant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt (so that the jury is sure).

bank.question: Under the Wills Act 1837, which TWO of the following are requirements for a will to be validly executed?
options: The testator must be at least 21 years of age.
The testator must be at least 18 years of age.
The will must be witnessed by at least one beneficiary.
The will must be signed by the testator in the presence of two or more witnesses present at the same time.
bank.explanation: For a valid will, the testator must be at least 18 years old and it must be signed in the presence of two witnesses who also sign in the testator's presence. Beneficiaries should not witness the will.
S.172 requires a director to act in good faith to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, while s.174 requires exercise of reasonable care, skill, and diligence.
options: Duty to promote the success of the company.
Duty to ensure the company makes a profit every financial year.
Duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence.
Duty to prioritize the interests of the majority shareholder over the minority.
bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, which TWO of the following are statutory duties owed by a director to the company?

bank.explanation: Under the Equality Act 2010, direct discrimination and harassment can never be objectively justified by an employer.
bank.question: Under the Equality Act 2010, which TWO of the following types of prohibited conduct can NEVER be objectively justified by an employer?
options: Direct discrimination
Indirect discrimination
Harassment
Discrimination arising from disability

bank.question: According to the Theft Act 1968, which TWO of the following are elements of the 'actus reus' of theft?
options: Dishonesty
Appropriation
Intention to permanently deprive
Property belonging to another
bank.explanation: Under section 1 of the Theft Act 1968, the actus reus requires the appropriation of property belonging to another. Intention and dishonesty are mens rea elements.

Section 174 of the Companies Act 2006 requires directors to exercise reasonable care, skill, and diligence based on both their actual knowledge (subjective) and what is expected of someone in their role (objective).
options: It is a statutory duty under the Companies Act 2006.
It includes an objective test of what is expected of a person in that role.
It includes a subjective test based on the specific director's actual knowledge and experience.
A director can exclude this duty by adding a clause to the Articles of Association.
bank.question: Identify THREE correct statements regarding a director's duty to exercise reasonable care, skill, and diligence.

bank.explanation: Private nuisance requires an interference with the use or enjoyment of land; a claimant must have a proprietary interest (e.g., owner or tenant), not just be a guest or mere licensee.
bank.question: In the law of private nuisance, which TWO of the following individuals would likely have the 'standing' to sue?
options: A guest staying at a hotel who is disturbed by noise.
A tenant under a three-year lease agreement.
A lodger with no exclusive possession of their room.
The registered freehold owner of the affected property.

bank.explanation: Under the Wills Act 1837, the marriage/civil partnership of a testator revokes a will unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage. Divorce does not revoke the will but treats the ex-spouse as having predeceased.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following events will automatically revoke a validly executed will in its entirety?
options: The testator enters into a new marriage or civil partnership.
The testator gets a divorce.
The testator physically destroys the will with the intention of revoking it.
An executor named in the will passes away.

bank.explanation: Section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 requires land contracts to be in writing, incorporate all agreed terms, and be signed by both parties. Seal is no longer required.
options: It must be executed as a deed under seal.
It must be in writing.
It must incorporate all the terms which the parties have expressly agreed.
It must be signed by or on behalf of each party to the contract.
bank.question: According to Section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, which THREE of the following are requirements for an enforceable contract for the sale of land?
Which TWO of the following examples would be classified as 'Hearsay' evidence in a criminal trial?
options: A witness testifying about what they heard a bystander say to prove the car hit the pedestrian.
A witness testifying that a defendant looked nervous.
A witness repeating a threat they heard to prove the victim's state of fear.
A written report by a doctor used as evidence of the injuries sustained by a victim.
bank.explanation: Hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted. If the statement is offered to prove state of mind or simply that the words were said, it is not hearsay.

bank.question: To create a valid express private trust, 'The Three Certainties' must be present. Which TWO of the following are part of this requirement?
options: Certainty of intention
Certainty of subject matter
Certainty of duration
Certainty of method
bank.explanation: A trust must have certainty of Intention, Subject matter (the property), and Objects (the beneficiaries). Method of distribution is not a 'certainty' requirement.
Specific performance is an equitable remedy used for unique items like land or rare antiques where damages would be inadequate. It is never used for personal service/employment contracts.
options: A contract for the sale of a mass-produced consumer electronic item.
A contract for the sale of a specific plot of land.
A contract for the sale of a one-of-a-kind Victorian painting.
An employment contract for a specialist surgeon.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following contracts are most likely to be enforced by the equitable remedy of 'Specific Performance'?

bank.explanation: Qualified privilege usually applies to legal or moral duties (e.g., employment references). Truth (justification) is a complete defense regardless of malice. Fair comment (honest opinion) is a separate defense.
bank.question: In a defamation claim, which TWO of the following would provide a complete defense to the defendant?
options: The statement made was substantially true.
The defendant was motivated by spite or malice.
The statement was made in a social media post intended for the public.
The statement was made in an employment reference provided to a prospective employer.

bank.explanation: A company is a separate legal person (Salomon v Salomon). Shares are transferable and the company continues to exist regardless of changes in membership (perpetual succession). Shareholders have limited liability.
bank.question: Which THREE of the following are fundamental characteristics of a UK private limited company (Ltd)?
options: The company has a separate legal personality from its members.
The company enjoys perpetual succession.
Shareholders generally have limited liability for the company's debts.
The company's assets are owned directly by the majority shareholder.

bank.question: Under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 (and Consumer Rights Act 2015), which TWO of the following terms are implied into a contract for the sale of goods?
options: The goods must be of satisfactory quality.
The goods must be the cheapest available for that description.
The goods must be fit for any particular purpose made known to the seller.
The goods must be delivered within 24 hours of the order.
bank.explanation: To be 'fit for purpose', the buyer must make the purpose known to the seller. For 'satisfactory quality', it is an implied term in all contracts where the seller acts in the course of business.

bank.question: Which TWO of the following are primary legal duties or powers of personal representatives during the administration of an estate?
options: To pay inheritance tax on the deceased's estate.
To rewrite the deceased's will if it is deemed unfair to the beneficiaries.
To sell or mortgage the deceased's property to satisfy debts.
To act as a guardian for the deceased's minor children indefinitely.
bank.explanation: Personal representatives are generally liable for inheritance tax on the deceased's estate and have the power to sell estate assets to pay debts and legacies.

bank.question: In a criminal trial in England and Wales, which TWO of the following statements accurately describe the general burden and standard of proof?
bank.explanation: In criminal proceedings, the general rule is that the burden of proof is on the prosecution and the standard is beyond reasonable doubt (though often phrased to juries as 'being sure').
options: The burden of proof is on the defendant.
The burden of proof is on the prosecution.
The standard of proof is on the balance of probabilities.
The standard of proof is beyond reasonable doubt/so that you are sure.

bank.question: Under the Law of Property Act 1925, which TWO of the following are the only types of legal estate that can exist in land?
bank.explanation: These are the two fundamental types of land ownership (legal estates) recognized under Section 1 of the Law of Property Act 1925.
options: Fee simple absolute in possession.
Term of years absolute.
A life interest under a trust of land.
An easement for a fixed period of time.

bank.question: Which TWO of the following are essential elements required for the formation of a legally binding contract in English Law?
bank.explanation: A valid contract requires an offer, acceptance, consideration, and the intention to create legal relations. Past performance is generally not valid consideration.
options: Offer and Acceptance.
Past consideration.
Intention to create legal relations.
A written document signed by both parties in all cases.

bank.explanation: Under TR1, a transfer can be made by 'Joint Tenants' (right of survivorship applies) or 'Tenants in Common' (shares pass via will/intestacy).
options: Hold the property on trust for themselves as beneficiaries in a life interest.
Hold the property on trust for themselves as joint tenants.
Hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares.
Hold the property as a corporation sole.
bank.question: When two people purchase a property together, which TWO common methods of holding the equitable interest are listed on the Land Registry TR1 form?
In criminal evidence, which TWO of the following best describe 'Hearsay' evidence?
options: Eye-witness testimony given directly from the witness box.
The defendant's own confession during a police interview.
An out-of-court statement made by a witness who has since died.
A statement made by a bystander not called to court, used to prove the facts contained in it.
bank.explanation: Hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted and is generally inadmissible in criminal trials unless an exception applies.
The main remedies for breach of contract are damages (compensatory) and equitable remedies like specific performance or injunctions. Penalties are not enforceable.
options: Punitive damages to punish the breaching party.
Compensatory damages to put the claimant in the position they would have been in.
Specific performance to compel the party to perform their obligations.
Automatic imprisonment for any breach of a commercial contract.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following are recognized remedies for a breach of contract in English Law?
Under the SRA Code of Conduct, in which TWO of the following situations must a solicitor generally refuse to act for a client?
options: The solicitor's own interests conflict with the client's interests.
The client is seeking advice on a matter that is technically difficult.
The solicitor's firm has too many other clients in unrelated sectors.
There is a conflict of interests between two or more current clients in the same matter.
bank.explanation: Under the SRA Code of Conduct, a solicitor must not act if there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, and must maintain independence.

bank.question: According to the Theft Act 1968, which TWO of the following are elements of the offence of Blackmail?
options: A peaceful request for a debt to be repaid.
An unwarranted demand.
The use of menaces.
Taking property without the intention to permanently deprive.
bank.explanation: Section 21 of the Theft Act 1968 defines blackmail as making an unwarranted demand with menaces with a view to gain or intent to cause loss.
A trust requires certainty of intention (words), certainty of subject matter (the property), and certainty of objects (the beneficiaries).
options: Certainty of Intention.
Certainty of Value.
Certainty of Subject Matter.
Certainty of Objects.
bank.question: To create a valid express private trust, which THREE of the following 'certainties' must be present?

options: The defendant must cause 'grievous bodily harm' for a simple assault.
Assault requires the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence.
Battery requires the actual application of unlawful force.
Assault and Battery are exactly the same legal concept and cannot be separated.
bank.explanation: Assault (creating fear of immediate violence) and Battery (application of unlawful force) are distinct common law offences often dealt with under the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following statements correctly distinguish between 'Assault' and 'Battery' as summary offences?

bank.explanation: Partners in a traditional partnership are agents of each other and have unlimited personal liability for the debts of the firm.
options: Liability for the debts of the partnership is unlimited.
Each partner acts as an agent for the partnership and the other partners.
Partners MUST be registered with Companies House to exist legally.
A partnership is a separate legal entity from its members.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following are characteristics of a traditional partnership under the Partnership Act 1890?

options: The testator subsequent marriage or civil partnership.
The testator being formally declared bankrupt.
The physical destruction of the will by the testator with the intention to revoke it.
A falling out between the testator and the primary beneficiary.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following events will generally result in the revocation of an existing will?
bank.explanation: Under the Wills Act 1837, a will is revoked by a later marriage/civil partnership or by destruction with the intention to revoke (animus revocandi).
Self-defence and duress are 'general' defences available to almost all crimes, whereas loss of control and diminished responsibility only reduce murder to manslaughter.
options: Loss of control.
Self-defence.
Diminished responsibility.
Duress by threats.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following are 'general defences' (available to most crimes) rather than 'partial defences' specific to murder?

options: The carrying on of a business.
The existence of a written Partnership Deed.
The business must be carried on in common by two or more people.
An intention to make a profit.
bank.question: Under the Partnership Act 1890, which THREE of the following are the statutory requirements for the existence of a partnership?
bank.explanation: Under S.1 of the 1890 Act, a partnership requires a business, carried on in common, with a view of profit. A formal deed is common but not legally required for formation.

bank.question: Which TWO of the following remedies are available 'at the court's discretion' rather than as a matter of legal right?
options: Equitable compensation.
Common law damages.
Prohibitory injunction.
Specific performance.
bank.explanation: Common law damages are available as of right for breach, while equitable remedies like injunctions are at the court's discretion.

bank.question: In a criminal case, which TWO of the following are considered 'procedural' or 'interlocutory' decisions rather than 'dispositive' final judgments?
options: Granting or withholding bail.
Delivering a verdict of guilty or not guilty.
Adjourning a case for a pre-sentence report.
Passing a custodial sentence.
bank.explanation: Adjournments and bail decisions are 'interlocutory' or 'procedural' steps, whereas a verdict follows the presentation of evidence.

bank.question: Under Section 8 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, which TWO conditions must be met for a Justice of the Peace to issue a search warrant?
options: The suspect has already been formally charged.
There are reasonable grounds to believe an indictable offence has been committed.
There is material on the premises likely to be of substantial value to the investigation.
The owner of the property has refused a voluntary search.
bank.explanation: For a search warrant, the police must show there are reasonable grounds to believe an indictable offence has been committed and that there is material on the premises likely to be of substantial value.
The SRA principles include acting with integrity, in a way that upholds public trust, and with independence. Profit maximization is not a core SRA Principle.
bank.question: Identify THREE SRA Core Principles that every solicitor must uphold when practicing law.
options: Act with integrity.
Act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the solicitors' profession.
Maximise the commercial interests of the law firm.
Act with independence.

bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, which TWO of the following are statutory duties specifically owed by a director to the company?
options: Exercise independent judgment.
Avoid conflicts of interest.
Ensure a dividend is paid to shareholders every year.
Act in the interests of the majority shareholder only.
bank.explanation: Directors owe duties to the company (the legal entity), which includes exercising independent judgment and avoiding conflicts. Shareholders exercise control via voting but don't owe these fiduciary duties.

options: The preferred interior paint colours of the tenant.
The identity of the landlord and tenant.
The duration of the term granted.
The amount of rent to be paid.
bank.question: Which THREE of the following are essential elements that must be defined for a leasehold interest to be validly created?
bank.explanation: A standard residential lease must typically specify the parties, the property, the term (duration), and the rent (consideration). The color of the decor is not a legal essential.

options: Interim payments.
Summary judgment.
Freezing injunctions.
Default judgment.
bank.question: Under the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR), which TWO of the following are classified specifically as 'Interim Remedies'?
bank.explanation: Interim payments and freezing injunctions are 'interim' remedies used before trial to preserve the status quo or assist the claimant. Summary judgment is an early final disposal.

bank.question: To secure a conviction for 'Theft', which TWO of the following elements must the prosecution prove?
options: Careless damage of the property.
Dishonest appropriation.
Intention to permanently deprive.
Temporary borrowing without consent.
bank.explanation: Section 1 of the Theft Act 1968 requires the dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with the intention to permanently deprive. Usage and damage are different offences.

bank.question: In the law of trusts and wills, which TWO of the following are examples of 'Vested' interests rather than 'Contingent' interests?
options: To my son, absolutely.
To my daughter, if she graduates from university.
To my wife for life, remainder to my son.
To my nephew, provided he survives me by 30 days.
bank.explanation: Vested interests are certain, whereas contingent interests depend on a condition (like reaching age 21 or marrying).
A public nuisance requires the act to materially affect the reasonable comfort and convenience of a class of Her Majesty's subjects.
bank.question: In the law of Tort, which TWO of the following must be proven for an individual to successfully sue for 'Public Nuisance'?
options: The act must affect a 'class of people' rather than a single individual.
The claimant must prove the defendant acted with specific intent to harm the environment.
The claimant must suffer 'special damage' over and above that suffered by the rest of the class.
Property ownership is a prerequisite for a claimant to bring an action in public nuisance.

bank.explanation: The three certainties (intention, subject matter, objects) are required for an express trust, but a trust of land must also be evidenced in writing under s.53(1)(b) LPA 1925.
bank.question: Which THREE of the following are legal requirements for the creation of a valid express inter vivos trust of land?
options: The trust must be executed as a deed.
The trust must be evidenced in writing signed by the settlor.
The trust must be registered at the Land Registry immediately to be valid.
The beneficiary must be identifiable with reasonable certainty.
The settlor must manifest a clear intention to create a trust.

bank.explanation: Voluntary manslaughter includes killings where the actus reus and mens rea of murder are present, but a partial defence applies.
options: Gross Negligence.
Diminished Responsibility.
Loss of Control.
Unlawful Act.
bank.question: Under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 and common law, which TWO of the following result in a conviction for 'Voluntary Manslaughter' rather than 'Involuntary Manslaughter'?

bank.explanation: Non-contentious probate (uncontested wills) and summary criminal trials are generally not covered by the 'loser pays' rule.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following types of legal proceedings generally do NOT follow the 'loser pays' rule for costs?
options: Small Claims Track cases (under £10,000).
Multi-track High Court commercial litigation.
Fast-track personal injury claims.
Criminal proceedings in the Magistrates' Court.

bank.explanation: Common law recognizes these three ways to sever a joint tenancy in equity, established in Williams v Hensman.
bank.question: According to the case of Williams v Hensman, which THREE of the following are methods by which a joint tenancy of land can be severed in equity?
options: An act operating on one's own share (e.g., selling or mortgaging the interest).
Registration of a Restriction at the Land Registry.
Mutual agreement between all of the joint tenants.
Unilateral oral declaration made by one joint tenant to the others.
A course of dealing sufficient to intimate that the interests of all were mutually treated as constituting a tenancy in common.

bank.explanation: Self-interest and Conflict of interest are distinct; a solicitor cannot act if there is a conflict or a significant risk of one.
bank.question: Under the SRA Code of Conduct, in which TWO of the following situations must a solicitor NOT act for a client?
options: When the solicitor has a personal relationship with the witness for the prosecution.
When there is a 'conflict of interest' between two or more current clients in the same matter.
When the solicitor's fee is paid by a third party.
When there is a 'significant risk' of a conflict between the interests of the solicitor and the client.

bank.explanation: Special damages cover specifically calculable financial losses, whereas general damages cover non-monetary losses like pain.
options: Loss of earnings from the date of the accident to the date of the trial.
The cost of repairing a damaged vehicle.
Pain, suffering, and loss of amenity (PSLA).
Future loss of earning capacity (Smith v Manchester award).
bank.question: In a personal injury claim, which TWO of the following are categorized as 'Special Damages'?

bank.explanation: Privilege is a fundamental right of the client; it is not lost through the death of the client or the mere suspicion of a crime.
bank.question: Which TWO of the following circumstances would result in Legal Advice Privilege being lost or inapplicable?
options: When the client dies and the executor waives the privilege.
When the legal advice is given by an unqualified paralegal supervised by a solicitor.
When the communication was made for the purpose of furthering a criminal or fraudulent design.
When the client gives express permission to waive the privilege.
Property includes 'money and all other property, real or personal, including things in action and other intangible property'.
The defendant must have intended to permanently deprive the owner at the moment they first touched the property.
Property shall be regarded as belonging to any person having possession or control of it, or having in it any proprietary right or interest.
Theft can be committed recklessly if the defendant knew there was a risk the property belonged to another.
bank.question: Under the Theft Act 1968, which TWO of the following statements regarding the definition of 'Property' and 'Belonging to Another' are correct?
bank.explanation: Section 1 of the Theft Act 1968 defines theft; 'belonging to another' includes possession or control, not just legal title.

bank.question: Which THREE of the following are true of a private limited company (Ltd) incorporated under the Companies Act 2006?
options: A private company must have at least two directors.
A private company is not required to have a company secretary.
A private company cannot offer its shares to the public.
A private company can be a 'single member' company.
A private company must hold an Annual General Meeting (AGM) every year by law.
bank.explanation: Private companies (Ltd) have fewer restrictions than public companies (Plc) regarding capital and management.

options: In commercial agreements, there is a strong presumption that the parties intended to create legal relations.
In domestic or social agreements, there is a rebuttable presumption that the parties did not intend to be legally bound.
A 'letters of comfort' is always legally binding as a matter of law.
An 'honour clause' in a contract makes the contract more enforceable in court.
bank.question: Regarding the 'Intention to Create Legal Relations' in contract law, which TWO of the following statements are correct?
bank.explanation: The rules on intention to create legal relations distinguish between social contexts (presumed no intent) and commercial ones (presumed intent).
Section 74 of the PACE Act allows for convictions of others to be used, but the court retains discretion to exclude evidence if it is unfair.
bank.question: In criminal trials, which TWO of the following statements accurately reflect the rules on 'Bad Character' evidence?
options: The prosecution can refer to a defendant's spent convictions under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 without leave.
The court has the power to exclude otherwise admissible prosecution evidence under Section 78 of PACE if it would have an adverse effect on the fairness of proceedings.
A defendant's previous convictions may be admissible if they are relevant to an important matter in issue between the defendant and the prosecution.
Character references must always be given under oath to be considered by the jury.
The prosecution must prove their case beyond reasonable doubt.
The prosecution must prove their case on the balance of probabilities.
A defendant raising a statutory defence usually carries the burden on the balance of probabilities.
The defendant must always prove their innocence beyond reasonable doubt.
bank.explanation: The standard of proof for the prosecution is 'beyond reasonable doubt' (or so that the jury are sure), while the burden of proof for a defendant raising a statutory defence is usually on the 'balance of probabilities'.
bank.question: In a criminal trial, which TWO of the following statements correctly describe the burden and standard of proof?

options: The defendant acted with malicious intent.
The defendant breached a duty of care owed to the claimant.
The claimant suffered damage that was not reasonably foreseeable.
The breach of duty caused the claimant's loss or injury.
bank.question: In a claim for negligence, which TWO of the following elements must the claimant prove to establish liability?
bank.explanation: For a claim in negligence, the claimant must prove that a duty of care was owed, this duty was breached, and that the breach caused reasonably foreseeable damage (causation and remoteness).

bank.question: Under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, in which THREE of the following scenarios is a solicitor generally prohibited from acting?
bank.explanation: Under the SRA Code of Conduct, solicitors must not act if there is a conflict of interest, a significant risk of one, or if their independence is compromised. Domestic disputes are not a per se bar unless a specific conflict arises.
options: There is a conflict between the interests of two or more current clients.
There is a conflict between the solicitor's own interests and those of the client.
The client is involved in a high-profile domestic dispute.
Acting would result in a breach of the solicitor's duty of confidentiality to a former client.

options: The risk of damage to the property passes to the buyer upon completion.
The risk of damage to the property passes to the buyer upon exchange of contracts.
The seller has a duty to manage the property with reasonable care between exchange and completion.

options: The 'Business Efficacy' test.
The 'Unfair Contract Terms' test.
The 'Reasonable Person' test.

bank.question: In a personal injury claim, which TWO of the following are examples of 'Special Damages'?
bank.explanation: Special damages relate to past, quantifiable financial losses (e.g., lost earnings and travel costs to date), whereas general damages are for non-monetary losses like pain and suffering.
options: An award for future loss of earnings.
An award for travel expenses incurred to attend medical appointments.
An award for loss of earnings from the date of the accident to the date of trial.
An award for pain, suffering, and loss of amenity (PSLA).

bank.question: Under the SRA Code of Conduct, which TWO of the following situations create a conflict that prevents a solicitor from representing a client in criminal litigation?
bank.explanation: A solicitor must not act for a client in a court proceeding if they know the client is going to commit perjury or if the solicitor's own independence is compromised, but they may act if the client simply has a criminal record.

bank.question: Regarding a solicitor’s duty of disclosure to their client, which THREE of the following are recognized exceptions where a solicitor does NOT have to disclose information?
bank.explanation: Solicitors have a duty to disclose all material information to a client, but exceptions apply if disclosure is prohibited by law (e.g., tipping off under AML rules), creates a risk of serious physical/mental harm, or it is a clear clerical error.

Which THREE of the following statements accurately describe the rules on Hearsay evidence in criminal proceedings?
bank.explanation: Hearsay is generally defined as an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted. In criminal trials, it is admissible if all parties agree, it is in the interests of justice, or a statutory exception applies.

bank.question: Which THREE of the following are characteristics of a valid charitable trust that distinguish it from a private express trust?
options: They may be established for a purpose rather than for identifiable individuals.
They are subject to the rule against inalienability (the common law rule against perpetuities).
They must be for the public benefit.
They are exempt from the requirement of certainty of objects.
bank.explanation: Private trusts must satisfy the 'beneficiary principle' and the rule against perpetuities, whereas charitable trusts can exist for a purpose and can last indefinitely.

bank.question: Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier, which TWO requirements must be met for beneficiaries to terminate a trust and demand the property?

bank.question: Under the Trustee Act 2000, which THREE of the following statements regarding a trustee's power of investment are correct?
bank.explanation: Trustees have broad powers to invest and delegate under the Trustee Act 2000, but they must act as a 'prudent person' would and consider the suitability of investments.

A Section 21 notice provides a 'no-fault' ground for possession.

bank.question: In relation to Assured Shorthold Tenancies (ASTs), which TWO of the following statements accurately describe the use of Section 8 and Section 21 notices?
bank.explanation: A Section 21 notice is for mandatory possession (no fault) after the fixed term; a Section 8 notice is used when the tenant has breached the agreement (fault).

bank.question: Under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, which TWO of the following statements regarding 'Bad Character' evidence are correct?
options: It is evidence of, or a disposition towards, misconduct.
It is always admissible if the defendant has a previous conviction for any offence.
It can be admitted if it is 'important explanatory evidence'.
It is only admissible if the defendant gives evidence in their own defence.
bank.explanation: Evidence of a defendant's bad character is generally inadmissible unless it falls under one of the 'gateways' in Section 101 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003.

bank.question: When determining the beneficial interests in a family home where the legal title is in joint names but there is no express declaration of trust, which TWO of the following describe the court's approach?

Under section 53(1)(c) of the Law of Property Act 1925, which TWO of the following requirements must be met for a valid disposition of a subsisting equitable interest?
options: The disposition must be made by a deed.
The disposition must be in writing.
An oral agreement witnessed by two solicitors is sufficient.
The disposition must be signed by the person disposing of the interest or their authorised agent.
bank.explanation: An oral agreement is insufficient for a disposition of an equitable interest; it must be in writing and signed by the person disposing of it under s53(1)(c) LPA 1925.

In criminal law, which TWO of the following statements regarding partial defences to murder are correct?
options: The defence of Provocation is currently available for murder charges.
Diminished Responsibility is a 'special' partial defence that only applies to a charge of murder.
Loss of control requires a 'qualifying trigger' as defined by the Coroners and Justice Act 2009.
Consent is a valid defence to a charge of Section 18 GBH if the victim is an adult.
bank.explanation: The defence of Provocation has been replaced by 'Loss of Control', and 'Special' defences like Diminished Responsibility only apply to murder, not all crimes.

bank.question: Regarding 'Strict Liability' offences in criminal law, which TWO of the following statements are correct?
options: The prosecution does not need to prove mens rea for at least one element of the actus reus.
The defendant cannot be imprisoned for a strict liability offence.
A 'mistake of fact' is always a valid defence to a strict liability offence.
These offences are often 'regulatory' in nature, such as environmental regulations.
bank.explanation: Strict liability offences do not require proof of mens rea for the actus reus, and often relate to quasi-criminal issues like environmental or road safety.

bank.question: Which THREE of the following are essential elements that a claimant must prove to succeed in a claim for the tort of negligence?
options: A pre-existing contract between the claimant and defendant.
A duty of care owed by the defendant to the claimant.
A breach of that duty of care by the defendant.
Legal advice taken by the claimant prior to the incident.
The breach caused the claimant's loss or injury (causation).
bank.explanation: The 4-stage test requires identifying the person, their duty, the breach, and that the breach caused the harm (causation).

bank.question: Under the SRA Principles, which TWO of the following are fundamental requirements for a solicitor's professional conduct?
options: Act with integrity.
Act in the best interests of the firm's profitability.
Act in the best interests of each client.
Always follow the client's instructions even if they involve illegal acts.
bank.explanation: The SRA principles override any conflict and require solicitors to act with integrity and in the best interests of each client.

bank.question: Under section 174 of the Companies Act 2006 (Duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence), which TWO of the following are used to assess the standard required?
bank.explanation: Under s.174 CA 2006, directors must exercise the care, skill, and diligence of a reasonably diligent person (objective) and use any special knowledge they actually possess (subjective).
options: A director only needs to show the skill of a typical person in the street.
The standard is that of a reasonably diligent person with the general knowledge/skill expected of someone in that role.
The standard is purely subjective based on the director's own belief.
The standard is increased if the director has specific professional qualifications or experience.

bank.question: To create a valid private express trust, 'The Three Certainties' must be satisfied. Which THREE of the following are those certainties?
options: Certainty of Intention.
Certainty of Subject Matter.
Certainty of Income.
Certainty of Objects.
bank.explanation: A trust must have a certain subject (property), object (beneficiaries), and the intention to create a trust to be valid.
